finding.claim: The DELETE /reports/:id handler calls the async authorize() without await, so the authorization check never gates the delete. Any caller with a session can delete any report. The rejected promise from a failed check is unhandled, which on Node 15+ can also crash the process.
finding.source: Any request with a session user (or none) sending DELETE /reports/:id with an arbitrary report id; the id comes from req.params.id.
finding.sink: db.reports.remove(report.id) at server.js:21, the protected delete operation.

trace.note: report is fetched by the attacker-supplied id with no ownership check
authorize(...) is called without await. The async function returns a Promise, and the 403 throw happens inside it, so the handler continues.
authorize is async. db.grants() is awaited, then the 403 error is thrown as a rejected promise that nobody awaits.
db.reports.remove runs immediately, before the grants check resolves
The handler returns 204, so the client sees success even when the user lacked the delete grant

finding.guards_checked: The PUT handler at line 27 correctly awaits authorize, which shows the intended control. The DELETE route has no try/catch and no other middleware or route-level authorization. The global middleware at lines 4-7 only copies req.session.user and does not check permissions. express.json() has no relevant effect. This file shows no other access control.

verdict.guard_found: authorize() at server.js:9-16 throws 403 inside an async function, but the DELETE handler at line 20 discards the returned promise; the global middleware at lines 4-7 only copies the session user. There is no try/catch and no other middleware or route-level check.
verdict.reason: server.js:20 calls authorize() without await, so the rejection at server.js:14 never blocks db.reports.remove at server.js:21, and the 204 at server.js:22 is returned; any session user can delete any report, unlike the PUT route at server.js:27, which awaits.

finding.claim: The PUT /reports/:id handler passes the raw request body to db.reports.update without field allowlisting (mass assignment). A user with only the 'write' grant could overwrite protected fields such as owner or id, or change grants-related fields, depending on the db layer. This needs the db implementation to confirm, and db is not defined in this repo.
finding.source: JSON body of PUT /reports/:id from a user holding the 'write' grant on the report.

trace.note: express.json() parses an attacker-controlled body into an arbitrary object
The authorize check passes for a user with write access
req.body is passed directly to update with no schema validation or field allowlist

finding.guards_checked: No validation, schema or allowlist is present in this file. The db layer is not in the repo, so any protection inside db.reports.update could not be checked. The authorize check at line 27 limits this to users with write access, so impact is restricted to privilege or field tampering by authorized writers.

verdict.guard_found: authorize() at server.js:9-16 (awaited at line 27, throws 403 without the 'write' grant). It does not restrict which fields are written. No allowlist or validation exists in this file, and the db layer is not in the repo.
verdict.reason: The trace is accurate (express.json at server.js:3, awaited authorize at :27, raw req.body passed to db.reports.update at :28), and a low-privilege writer can reach it with no field filtering in this file. Whether protected fields like owner or id can be overwritten depends on the undefined db.reports.update implementation, so the finding cannot be confirmed or refuted from this repo.
